overview: Two essential experimental checks — one confirms the test can detect a true positive, the other confirms it doesn't falsely detect one.
genZNote: Positive control: proving your test CAN say yes. Negative control: proving your test won't say yes when it shouldn't.

aspects.label: Expected Result
aspects.valueA: Known to give a positive/expected result, confirming the assay is working correctly.
aspects.valueB: Known to give a negative result, confirming there's no contamination or false signal.

aspects.label: Purpose
aspects.valueA: Validates that the test system can detect a true positive.
aspects.valueB: Validates that the test system does not produce a false positive.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: A known antibiotic-sensitive strain in a disk diffusion assay.
aspects.valueB: Sterile broth with no bacteria added, checking for contamination.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: A valid experiment needs both controls together — a positive result without a negative control run in parallel can't rule out contamination.
overlay.memoryTrick: Positive control should test positive. Negative control should test negative — if either fails, the whole experiment is in question.
overlay.commonMisconception: A positive control is not the same as the actual experimental sample — it's a separate, known reference used purely to validate the test system.
